memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "They built the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood, three cubits high; it was square, five cubits long and five cubits wide." - Exod 38:1 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The first thing anyone entering the courtyard would meet was the altar of burnt offering. Not the beautiful lampstand. Not the gold-covered table. An altar, where animals died.

The order matters. Before there was fellowship, there was sacrifice. Before anyone went further in, blood was shed at the gate.

That is not an accident of layout; it is the gospel written into architecture. Sin cannot simply be waved away. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (Heb 9:22).

We live in a time that finds this offensive. Why not just forgive? But we sense the answer ourselves whenever we are genuinely wronged. A judge who releases the guilty without addressing the crime is not merciful; he is corrupt. God's forgiveness is costly precisely because His justice is real.

Notice the altar's size. Five cubits square — roughly two and a half metres each way. Large, prominent, unavoidable, standing in the open courtyard where everyone could see it.

God did not hide the cost of approaching Him. And He has not hidden it since. At the centre of Christian faith stands a cross — public, brutal, and outside the city gate.

Everything else in the tabernacle stood behind that altar. Everything in our lives stands behind that cross.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you tend to minimise the cost of your forgiveness?
2. Why do you think God placed the altar first, in plain sight?
3. What difference does it make that the cross was public rather than private?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, thank You that You did not forgive me cheaply. Keep the cross central in how I see everything. Amen.
